title: Minehan asks how much faster America can grow before prices rise
summary: Boston Fed President Cathy Minehan saw a reasonable chance that US growth could slow from above 4% and carry on expanding. The difficult judgement in her 6 January Hartford speech was how much slowing the economy needed. The United States had averaged roughly 4% growth since 1995, created over 13.6 million jobs and pushed unemployment to a thirty-year low. Even with oil prices up, inflation was running in the mid-2% range. Taking the low inflation reading at face value could lead policymakers to underestimate demand. Treating all the rapid growth as excess demand could needlessly cut short employment gains that higher productivity had made possible.

Minehan put numbers on both sides. With labour force participation broadly stable, population growth was supporting workforce growth of roughly 1% a year. Productivity had also risen about 1% annually in the late 1980s and early 1990s, when a common estimate of sustainable GDP growth was 2–2½%. From 1996, productivity had averaged roughly 2½%, with still faster increases in 1998 and 1999. Real spending on information processing equipment and software had grown about 21% a year since 1996. That was a credible reason for firms to produce more per hour, particularly when investment allowed them to redesign work. But in a boom, employees can work more intensively for a time. Both changes appear as stronger measured productivity. Only the first would support the same increase in output through a full business cycle.

Even granting that all the recent productivity improvement would last, Minehan saw actual GDP growth of more than 4% outstripping sustainable growth of more than 3%. Unemployment was still declining. Her concern therefore survived a relatively optimistic assumption about technology. Equally, she stopped short of treating the difference as a precise output gap. The figures compare growth rates, while the amount of spare capacity at any point depends on the starting level of output and employment. She drew on the continuing tightening of labour markets as additional evidence that the difference mattered.

Several developments could explain why higher inflation had been slow to appear. Weak growth overseas had attracted funds to the United States, helped finance the external deficit and supported the dollar. Cheaper imports constrained domestic producers' prices. Weak world demand also held down commodity costs, while healthcare restructuring restrained benefits costs for US employers. By January, oil and insurance premiums were rising and the Asian recovery was strengthening demand for US exports. That recovery had two implications for the US outlook. It could lift manufacturing orders just as it gave investors more alternatives to US assets. Domestic spending could still draw support from appreciating, if volatile, household wealth. The speech reports these channels without estimating the size of a dollar or equity-market response.

She also identified reasons that inflation or rates might rise less than those trends suggested. Firms reported little pricing power, public budgets were in surplus and earlier monetary tightening had yet to work fully through the economy. She saw tentative softness in interest-sensitive markets but wanted more observations before treating it as a trend. The policy signal was a concern about upside inflation risk alongside a willingness to let the tightening already delivered take effect. It represents a regional Reserve Bank president's assessment. The speech specified neither the size nor the timing of a subsequent policy move.

New England offered a way to check the national reading against the experience of an earlier boom. The region's labour force was growing relatively slowly, so very low unemployment could reflect limited labour supply as well as unusually strong demand. In the late 1980s a property and construction boom had obscured weakness in manufacturing. In early 2000, despite prominent building projects, construction employment was only around two-thirds to three-quarters of its 1988 peak. Manufacturing job losses tracked the national pattern and local wages showed less pressure than in the earlier boom. Minehan judged the region increasingly exposed to the same capacity constraints as the country, with less evidence of a distinct regional property cycle.

The millennium changeover mattered for interpreting incoming data. Nearly 33 million people were due almost $22 billion in direct Social Security deposits on 3 January. Tests had shown that an uncorrected Reserve Bank system would reject the dated file. The roughly $125 million that Reserve Banks expected to spend over three years included staff reassigned from other projects and equipment they would eventually have bought. A successful payment run was evidence that the repairs worked. The expenditure total alone said little about economy-wide demand. Minehan also saw little evidence of the anticipated year-end inventory surge or an interruption to electronic equipment orders, weakening the case for a mechanical reversal in first-quarter activity.

questions.question: How much of the productivity acceleration could a policymaker reasonably have treated as durable in January 2000?
questions.detail: Reconstruct quarterly output, hours and investment from releases available by the speech date. Compare industries investing heavily in information technology with other industries at similar points in their production cycles. Persistent gains after hours and utilisation normalise would support the higher-capacity reading. If gains concentrate in peak-demand quarters or appear mainly after statistical revisions, the contemporaneous case for raising potential growth becomes weaker.

questions.question: Would an unwinding of temporary cost relief first appear in import prices, compensation or underlying domestic inflation?
questions.detail: Track exchange-rate-adjusted import prices, oil, employers' benefit costs, unit labour costs and industry selling prices separately. The ordering matters. An energy spike can lift headline inflation while foreign competition still restrains domestic pricing. A broad increase in unit costs and selling prices as import competition fades would give the tight labour market greater weight in interpreting future inflation releases.

questions.question: Was the earlier monetary tightening slowing final demand quickly enough to accommodate less spare capacity?
questions.detail: Compare the sequence of housing activity, orders for durable goods, consumer spending and credit conditions with export orders and the rebuilding of inventories after the date change. Distinguish declines concentrated in rate-sensitive purchases from a temporary rotation into other categories. A regional comparison should allow for New England's slower labour-force growth and smaller construction workforce before interpreting unusually low unemployment as excess demand.
